_howto: Newest first. Add an entry at the top each time you push an update; the website and the game's title screen both read this file. tag: new | improved | fixed. roadmap status: done | testing | next | planned.

notes.title: Your own program in a league with friends

items.text: Call-ups in a league with friends. Open the league book, go to your program and call a junior varsity player up, six at most. It counts from the next game you open, and it has the same price as in a solo dynasty.
Your own spring practice. When the season ends, each coach picks what his school works on before the commissioner starts the next year. A coach who picks nothing gets what the league decides.
Job offers and the banquet and signing-day pages are still solo only.

notes.title: Leagues with friends catch up

items.text: A league with friends now keeps everything a solo dynasty does: every player's statistics, each school's record book, the season awards, the rivalries and their trophies, injuries and team news, and the weekly paper.

League book. From the league page, open the league as a dynasty to read: your school's season page, your program, the statistics, the record books, the awards and the paper. Nothing in it can change the league.
The four-team playoff comes to leagues with friends: semifinals, then the championship.
Injuries, ineligibility and suspensions now apply in league games you coach as well as simulated ones, so the team you take the field with is the team the league page says you have.

A league that is already running finishes its current season the old way and gets the playoff from its next season. Its statistics start from the next game played; games already played are not counted.
Still solo only: call-ups, choosing your own spring practice, job offers and the off-season pages. In a league with friends each school's spring work is decided by the league.

notes.title: Playoffs, and fewer injuries

items.text: A four-team playoff. The top four in the standings play on: first hosts fourth and second hosts third in the semifinals, and the winners meet for the championship at the home of the higher finisher.
The dynasty page shows the bracket, and a dashed line under fourth place in the standings marks who is in.
Playoff wins and losses count in your record. The paper prints a semifinals edition before the championship edition.

Injuries are about half as common: around two a program a season instead of four. The serious ones are rarer still: about one injury in seventeen ends a season, and about one in four hundred ends a career.

A dynasty you already have finishes its current season the old way, first against second, and gets the bracket from its next season. Nothing in an existing save is changed. Leagues with friends still end with first against second for now.

notes.title: A phone check

items.text: Every main page was checked at phone width: nothing scrolls sideways. The drive chart in the game book now fits a phone screen.

notes.title: The off-season

items.text: A full off-season between seasons, one stop at a time: awards banquet, signing day, the coaching carousel, spring practice and fall camp.
Awards banquet: your team's most valuable players on offense and defense and its best young player, alongside the league awards.
Signing day: where your seniors are going to play in college. Most are done with football; a program sends two or three on in a typical year, and a Division I signing is rare.
Coaching carousel: after a winning season or a title, schools that had a losing year may call with a job. Your career record goes with you. Nobody is ever fired.
Spring practice: choose what the team works on. Strength, speed, the passing game or fundamentals. Every returning player comes back a point better in it.
Fall camp: who left over the summer, who walked on, who transferred in, and the freshmen to watch.
Call-ups now have a price. A player who still needs your call at the end of the season spent the year on the sideline instead of playing junior varsity, and comes back a rating point short for good.
Other schools hold spring practice too; what each works on is decided by the league, not by you.

notes.title: Rivalries and the Saturday paper

items.text: Every school has a rival. They meet in the last week of the regular season, every year, and play for a trophy with a name of its own.
Each rivalry has fifty years behind it: an all-time series that is never far from level, and one school holding the trophy when you arrive. Your games add to it.
Beating your rival is worth a little extra to your program the next year, on top of the win.
Rivalry week is announced on the dynasty page, the game opens with a rivalry banner, and a win ends with one.

The weekly paper. After each week, read the state's prep sports page: your game leads, every other game gets a headline and the night's best player, with the standings, a notebook of records and injuries, and what is coming next.
A championship edition closes the season with the title game and the player of the year.

notes.title: The game book: box score, drives and play-by-play

items.text: A game book after every game, with four tabs. Summary: points by quarter, every scoring play and the team totals, now with third and fourth downs, penalties, punts and time of possession.
Box score: every player's line for both teams. Passing, rushing, receiving, defense, kicking and returns.
Drives: every possession, where it started, how many plays and yards, how long it took and how it ended.
Play-by-play: every snap of the game with down, distance and spot, quarter by quarter.
In a dynasty, open the game book for any of last week's games between other schools from the results list.
The book for a game you coached is on the final screen that night; it is not kept afterwards yet.

notes.title: Injuries, walk-ons, phenoms, and a new main menu

items.text: Injuries. A few players in every program get hurt each season. Most miss a game or two, some are lost for the year, and once in a great while an injury ends a career. A player who is out does not dress, and the next man at his position moves up.
Grades and discipline. When report cards come out in mid-season a player can be ruled academically ineligible for two or three games, and now and then someone is suspended for a game or two.
Kids move. A family can move away during the season, and over the summer a player or two may transfer out or give the game up.
Walk-ons. One to three players turn up at fall camp every year from the soccer team, the track team, the band. Most are depth; about one in eight can really play.
Transfers in. Some years a player transfers into your school.
Phenoms. About one freshman class in eight has a player with senior-level talent on the day he arrives. He is flagged in your program so you can decide whether to call him up.
Team news on the dynasty page: the injury report and the comings and goings at your school, and anything big from around the league. Before each game you are told who is not dressing.
A new main menu on wide screens: the sunset kickoff picture with the six choices down the right side. Phones keep the stacked menu.

Injuries are decided between games for now; nobody is carried off during a game you are coaching. All of this applies to solo dynasties. In a league with friends, players can leave between seasons and walk-ons arrive, but nobody is sidelined in season yet.

notes.title: Closer to real Friday nights, and more of the art on the field

items.text: Scoring is up. The clock runs a little less between plays, so each team gets about five more snaps a game and even games average about 20 points a team instead of 19.

Strong schools and weak schools are further apart. In a league, about four games in ten are now decided by three scores or more (it was fewer than two in ten; real high school football is over five), and the average is about 21 points a team.
Home field counts. The home side now wins about 55 percent of league games, the same as real results.
To keep leagues from being run by one school for ever, programs drift back toward the middle a little faster between seasons.
Runs look like runs. On a run the quarterback turns and hands the ball to the back; he no longer sets up as if to throw first.
A flag on the play: yellow penalty flags are thrown across the screen and land on the field.
Running back art: a lowered shoulder for a truck, a hard cut for a juke, and a full-stretch dive at the goal line.
Receiver art: a receiver lays out for a pass he cannot reach, and the scorer spikes the ball after a touchdown.
Special teams art: the returner settles under the kick with his hands up before he takes off.

Defense art: linebackers and the secondary wait in a crouch, the tackler is laid out where he made the stop, a defender has his hand up after knocking a pass away, and an interceptor goes up with the ball.
Quarterback art: the handoff uses the new handoff picture, ball held out to the back.

Eleven more arcade-style panels and signs: a runner bursting into the open and a stiff arm for runs of 20 yards or more, a leaping catch and a quarterback's throw for long passes, a pile-up for fumbles, the referee's signal and a TOUCHDOWN sign, cheerleaders after an extra point, and FUMBLE, INTERCEPTED and SACK signs.
A dynasty already under way keeps its results, records and stats; its rosters shift a little because of the wider gap between schools.

notes.title: Saves that follow you, linemen in their stances, and a crowd with feelings

items.text: Permanent saves. Sign in with a coach name and a four-digit PIN (the same one you use to play online) and your dynasty, your designed plays and your playbook are kept on the server every time they change.
Sign in with the same name on another device and your dynasty is there. Play a week on your phone and the laptop picks it up the next time you open the game.
An older copy never quietly overwrites a newer one. If a device has a dynasty of its own that differs from the one on the server, the game shows you both and asks which to keep.
Save files. Download your save as a file to keep, and load it back on any device, signed in or not.
A Saves page on the main menu shows where your save is and when it was last saved.
Linemen line up like linemen. Both lines get down in a three-point stance facing each other across the ball, and drive into their man at the snap, using the linemen art pack.
The crowd shows how it feels. Faces pop up out of the stands after the plays that matter: celebrating when the home team scores or takes the ball away, groaning when the visitors do.
One save per coach name for now. Saving to the server works on the website; the preview build cannot reach the server, but save files still load there.

notes.title: Weather you can see, a homecoming court, and new story panels

items.text: Rain, snow and wind now use the drawn weather art. Rain falls in slanted streaks, snow drifts down in flakes, and on a windy night leaves blow across the field.
A low mist drifts across the field behind the rain and the snow.
On homecoming night the court walks out at halftime: a king and queen, four attendants and a banner, standing with the band.
A panel before the kickoff. At home your team bursts through the paper banner; on the road the bus pulls in under the lights; on homecoming night the homecoming banner goes up.

More panels through the night: a banner for the start of the fourth quarter, a coin toss or banner for overtime, the locker room and the chalkboard at half time, and the coaches' handshake after a loss.
There is no fog-only weather in the game yet, so the fog art shows as the mist in rain and snow. That finishes the list of looks; saves that follow you between devices are next.

notes.title: A field that wears, and players who block, catch and spin

items.text: The field wears as the game goes on. Turf scuffs along the line of scrimmage and where runners go down, so the fourth quarter looks different from the kickoff.
In the rain the field churns to mud and puddles form. In snow the field starts white and gets trampled back to green where the plays go.
More poses. Linemen and blockers stand up with their hands out once the ball is snapped, a receiver puts his hands up as the ball arrives, and a runner who spins or jukes turns as he does it.
A referee on the field. He stands behind the offense, puts his arms up for a touchdown, points for a first down and throws the flag on a penalty.
Cheerleaders at each end of the sideline in their school's colours. They go wild when their team scores.
Louder call-outs. A juke, spin, stiff arm, truck or dive now pops up over the runner as a big tilted word in its own colour, with his number.
Feelings. Now and then a small emoji floats up from a player or a bench: joy at a touchdown, despair at a turnover, a flexed arm after a sack, a facepalm at a flag.
The band takes the field at half time: drum major out front, colour guard on the wings, brass, sousaphones and the drum line behind, all in the home school's colours.
Kicking units. The punter punts, and on a field goal or extra point a holder goes down on one knee with the ball.
The marks come from the plays themselves, so a game you rejoin shows the same field.

Yard lines that looked uneven. The sharper field was being squeezed to fit the screen with hard edges, which made some lines fat, some thin and some crooked. It is now scaled smoothly, so every line is the same.

notes.title: Big-moment panels and paint on the grass

items.text: New pop-up panels for big moments: a touchdown spike and a dive for the pylon, "Loose ball!" on a fumble, "No good!" on a missed kick, a blocked kick, and a second interception panel.
Win a game and your players celebrate with the coach. Win the state final and you get the trophy. Half time on homecoming night shows the king and queen being crowned.

The stands are rebuilt from the front-view stadium art: one long bleacher with the home crowd and the band in the middle, thin visitors' ends, a press tower at midfield and a scoreboard. Nothing overlaps.
Paint on the grass: each school's name in its end zone and the home team's letters at midfield.

notes.title: New players, a real stadium and a sideline

items.text: New players on the field, cut from the new sprite sheets and repainted in each school's jersey, helmet and pants colours. They run with a four-frame stride, set in a stance before the snap and go to ground when tackled.
Poses. The quarterback sets and throws, a runner who stiff-arms or trucks a tackler shows it, the kicker swings his leg, and the team that scores a touchdown throws its arms up.
A stadium behind the field: bleachers full of fans, a press box at midfield, and a wall of local sponsors' boards.
A sideline in front of it: each team's bench, players standing, and coaches, all in the school's colours.
The chain crew. Two sticks mark the ten yards and the down box follows the ball, showing the down.
The field is drawn at twice the resolution, so sprites and boards are sharp on big screens.
Still to come from the new art: catching poses, line play, juke and spin animations, field goal units, injuries, referees, cheerleaders, the band and the homecoming court.

notes.title: Season awards

items.text: Awards. When the title game is over the league votes a player of the year, a defensive player of the year, a newcomer of the year (the best freshman or sophomore) and an all-league team of sixteen.
Coach of the year goes to the school that most beat expectations, so winning five games at a rebuilding school counts for more than winning six at a powerhouse.
An Awards page keeps every season's winners, and each school's record book now lists its honors: award winners and all-league players by year.
Awards are voted from the season's statistics, so they are in solo dynasty for now.

notes.title: Statistics, school records and a new look

items.text: Statistics. Every game in a dynasty now keeps a box score for every player at all eight schools: passing, rushing, receiving, tackles, sacks, interceptions and kicking. The Statistics page shows your team's leaders and the league leaders.

School record books. Each school has records for a single game, a season and a career, and the book is already full when you arrive: fifty years of names and numbers. Beat one and your player's name goes in.

Record watch. During your own games the bench tells you when a player is closing in on a school record, and the moment one falls it is called on the field and by the announcer. Season and career records are settled when the season ends.
Records that fall anywhere in the league show up on the dynasty screen, and you can open any school's record book.
The final screen of every game names each team's leaders: passer, runner, receiver and tackler.

A new look everywhere, taken from the scoreboard and start-screen art: pixel lettering, gold frames for the home side and blue for the visitors, and larger text on the call sheet, the dynasty pages and the menus.
Statistics and records are in solo dynasty. A dynasty saved before this update starts its statistics from its next game.

notes.title: A real main menu, and schools that are hiring

items.text: Main menu. Exhibition, Dynasty, Play online, Playbook and Hall of Fame each get their own row, built from the new start-screen art. Press 1 to 5 to pick one and Esc to come back.
Exhibition and Play online now have their own pages instead of sharing one crowded screen.

Starting a dynasty is a job hunt. Pick a state and five of its eight schools are looking for a head coach. Each posting tells you why the job is open, last season's record, how many seniors are back, the best player and what the school expects.
The huddle. Between plays both teams huddle up while you pick. Your offense breaks to the line when the call is made.
The announcer now uses the most natural voice your browser has, at a normal pitch. How good it sounds still depends on your phone or computer.
Removed the crowd noise. It sounded like waves. The "de-fense" chant, the claps and the band stay.

The jump when a kick was caught. Players used to snap to new spots as the return began. Now everyone runs to where the return starts while the ball is in the air, and the ball comes down on the returner.
Punts and field goals are kicked from a formation, not from the huddle.

notes.title: Friday night atmosphere

items.text: Chants. "De-fense" with stomps when the visitors have to convert, and a clap-along when the home team is driving.

A pep band. Every school has its own fight song, made from the school itself so it is always the same tune. The band plays it after home touchdowns, at half time and after a home win, with a drum line underneath and a horn stab on first downs.
A public address announcer calls touchdowns, turnovers, some first downs, the half-time score and the final. It has its own on/off button next to Sound.

Half-time shows. Every game has one: a band set and something happening on the field. In a dynasty each school's home schedule has a home opener, homecoming and senior night. Homecoming crowns a king from your senior class and a queen; senior night honors your seniors by name. The title game has both bands.
The dynasty screen tells you when this week is homecoming, senior night or a home opener.
All of the sound is generated on the spot. There are no audio files.

notes.title: Freshmen, JV and varsity

items.text: Every school now has a real program: four classes of 22, freshman to senior. The same players come back a year older and better each season, seniors graduate, and a new freshman class arrives.
Varsity and junior varsity. You coach the 39-man varsity on Friday. The other 49 play JV on Thursday against the same opponent, and you see their score and record.
Call-ups. Open Your program in a dynasty and call up to six JV players to the varsity. The weakest varsity player at that position goes down in his place. Send a call-up back down any time.
Each player shows his rating now and what he should be as a senior, so you can spot the freshman worth waiting for. Class years also show on the sideline depth chart.
When a season ends the program page lists the seniors you are losing and the freshmen to watch.

Varsity teams are built to the same strength as before, so dynasty scores have not moved. Underclassmen have to be clearly better to take an upperclassman's place: about nine varsity players in ten are juniors or seniors.
Call-ups are in solo dynasty for now. Leagues with friends use the same aging rosters, with the varsity picked on merit.
A dynasty saved before this update keeps its record and schedule but gets new rosters.

notes.title: Audibles and ball-carrier moves

items.text: Audibles. Call your play and your offense walks to the line. The defense shows its front (never its call), and you can snap it or change to any other play from the same formation.
Audibles work online too. Both calls go in, then the offense gets eight seconds at the line. The other coach sees only that you are at the line, and his call is locked.
The AI quarterback checks at the line as well: out of a run into a loaded box, or into a run against a light one. It happens a few times a game.

Ball-carrier moves. A missed tackle is now a stiff arm, a truck, a juke or a spin, picked by the runner's power and agility, and a runner who falls forward for extra yards dives. Backs, receivers after the catch, and returners all have them, with a callout on the field.
Changing the play at the line is noisy: a false start is almost twice as likely on an audible.
Moves name what already happened on a broken tackle. They do not change how often tackles are broken.

notes.title: Returns: kicks, punts, picks and fumbles

items.text: Interceptions and fumble recoveries are run back. The defender takes off from where he got the ball, his teammates block, and the offense has to chase him down. Some go all the way.
Kickoff and punt returns are now real plays: a returner, blockers who pick up the coverage, missed tackles and the occasional touchdown.
Special teams tab on the call sheet. On fourth down it opens by itself with Punt, Field goal and Fake it. Fake it lets you line up to kick and run a real play.
Return touchdowns are rare: about one turnover in fourteen is taken to the house, and a kickoff goes the distance well under once in a hundred.
Instant replay shows the play, not the return that followed it.

notes.title: Real football: flags, a run-first game and commissioner tools

items.text: Penalties. False starts and offside before the snap, holding and pass interference on the play. A hold brings the gain back; interference is fifteen yards and a first down.
Commissioners can rename any school and pick its jersey, helmet, pants and trim colors, in a league with friends or in a solo dynasty. The school keeps its players, strength and record.
Kick and punt returns are run back on the field: the returner fields the ball, blockers set up in front of him and the coverage closes in.
AI coaches now call a high school game: about six plays in ten are runs, they go for it more on fourth down, and kickers are high school kickers, good to about 40 yards.
More sacks, more fumbles, fewer field goals. Quarterbacks hold the ball a beat longer under pressure.
A realism scorecard now checks every change against 16 real-football numbers over 150 AI games, from yards per carry to penalties per team.
Because the football changed, games play out differently from earlier versions with the same calls.

notes.title: Overtime

items.text: Overtime. A game level after four quarters goes to high school overtime: each team gets the ball first and goal at the ten. Still level, they go again, and the team that went second goes first.
The AI coach takes the field goal on fourth down in overtime unless only a touchdown keeps the game alive, and never punts.
After four overtime periods a game still level ends as a tie. In a dynasty title game that tie goes to the home team.

notes.title: Dynasty with friends

items.text: Dynasty with friends. Sign in, start a league in any state and share its five-letter code. Each friend takes a school; the AI runs the rest.
When two coaches meet, both have to be there. The first to arrive waits in the game room and it kicks off the moment the second sits down. Voice chat works in league games too.
Games against AI schools can be played whenever you like. Games between two AI schools play themselves.
The week moves on when every game is in. If someone is away, the commissioner can let the AI finish the week.
Win the state title in a shared league and it goes on your coach profile as a championship.
Tackles no longer make the ball carrier jump forward. He now drives ahead with the tackler on him and goes down at the spot.
League games against AI schools count in the league but not in the Hall of Fame, which is for games between two coaches.

notes.title: Dynasty, special teams, weather and cut-ins

items.text: Dynasty. Pick any of the fifty states and one of eight invented schools. Play seven league games, then first plays second for the state title. Coach each game yourself or let your assistant handle it.
Seasons roll on: winners get a little stronger, everyone drifts back toward the pack, rosters turn over, and your trophy case and career record are kept.
Kickoff calls: kick deep, squib it, or try an onside kick. A surprise onside is recovered about one time in four; when they expect it, about one in nine.

Go for the block. On fourth down the defense can sell out against a punt or field goal: a chance to block it, a risk of a flag. If the offense fakes it and runs a real play, the defense is caught out of position.
Game length. Choose 4, 6, 8, 10 or 12 minute quarters before kickoff. The host chooses for online games.
Weather. Rain, wind, snow and heat change catching, deep throws, fumbles, kicking and how fast players tire. In a dynasty the forecast depends on the state and the week.
Cut-ins. Touchdowns, interceptions, sacks, safeties, kicks, half time and the final whistle get their own artwork.
New screenshots on this site.
Dynasty is solo for now: your league is saved in this browser. Dynasties with friends coaching rival schools are next, and games between two coaches will need both online.
There is no overtime yet. A tied league game stays a tie; a tied championship goes to the home team.

notes.title: The big playbook: 40 on offense, 40 on defense

items.text: Your starter book is now 40 offensive plays: eight from each of the five formations. Sixteen plays are new, including Stretch, Fullback Dive, Play-Action Post, Tunnel Screen, Corner Shot, Double Slants, Fades, Bootleg and Max Protect Shot.
Call offense by formation: pick Singleback, I-Form, Shotgun, Spread or Heavy (keys Z X C V B), then the play.
40 defensive calls: a new 4-4 front joins the 4-3, 5-2, Nickel and 3-4, and each front can now run eight calls. New calls: Man Free, Cover 2, Zone Blitz and Prevent.
Books can hold 8 to 52 plays, so your own designs go on top of the 40 instead of replacing them. Trim the book if you like a shorter call sheet.
The AI coach uses the whole book and the new defenses, and saves Prevent for protecting a late lead.
Saved playbooks from older versions are reset to the new 40-play starter book. Your designed plays and defenses are kept.
Special teams calls (onside and squib kicks, fakes, going for the block) are next, along with the new cut-in artwork.

notes.title: Design your own plays, coach records and the Hall of Fame

items.text: Play designer. Open Edit playbook and press Design a play: drag your eleven into place, give each player a job, and click the field to draw routes and running lanes.
Defense designer. Place your eleven defenders and tell each one to rush, cover a man, drop to a zone or read the play.
The game checks every design against the rules and tells you in plain words what to fix, such as too few players on the line.
Practice field. Run a design dozens of times against any defense (or any play) and see average gain, completions, sacks and turnovers. Watch one to see it on the real field.
Keep up to 12 plays and 6 defenses of your own. Your plays go in your eight-play book; your defenses are under the Mine tab on defense.
Your designs come with you into online games. The server checks them again, and both coaches see the same play.
Coach profile. Every finished online game counts toward your career wins, losses, points and best winning streak. Championships will count once dynasty seasons arrive.
Hall of Fame. The ten best records among all online coaches, one button from the menu.
Coverage now lines up against the formation in front of it, so corners follow receivers wherever you put them.
Known gap: a very carefully built custom play can still gain more than it should against the AI. Tightening that is ongoing.

notes.title: Sideline voice chat

items.text: Talk to the other coach during an online game. Press Voice chat in the lobby or on the sideline bar and allow your microphone.
Audio goes straight from one browser to the other. It never passes through the game server, and it is free.
Mute your mic at any time; the status line shows whether you are connected. Voice carries on from the lobby into the game.

notes.title: Online head-to-head

items.text: Play a friend online. Sign in with a coach name and a four-digit PIN, host a game, and share the five-digit game PIN. The other coach types it in to join.
Hidden play calls: you only see that the other sideline has called its play, never what it is, until the snap.
The server runs every play. Both browsers replay it from the shared record and check that they match the server exactly.
If a coach drops out, the AI calls his plays so nobody is left waiting. He can sign back in on any device and pick up where the game is.
Depth chart and game plan changes work online, and your own eight-play book comes with you.
The site now publishes itself when an update is merged.

notes.title: Playbooks, fronts and the sideline

items.text: A 24-play library across five formations: Singleback, I-Form, Shotgun, Spread and Heavy, with lead blockers, quarterback runs and a sneak.
Build your own playbook: pick the eight plays you carry into the game. Your book is remembered on your device.
Four defensive fronts (4-3, 5-2, Nickel, 3-4), each with four calls. Man coverage now matches up against whatever formation lines up.
Full 39-player rosters with depth charts. Players tire as they play, slow down, and are rested automatically; reorder your depth chart from the sideline.
A 20-second play clock. If it runs out, your AI coach makes the call from your game plan: run or pass lean, and how bold to be on fourth down.
Kneel-downs to run out the clock.
A sharper AI coach: kneels to finish a win, plays prevent defense with a late lead, brings the heavy front on the goal line and chases two points when the score calls for it.
Balance: over 200 simulated games, no play averages more than 1.5 times the playbook average, and a wrong defensive guess hurts without deciding the game.

notes.title: Start screen, logo and this site

items.text: Friday Night Dynasty start screen and logo.
This website, with dev notes and the roadmap. The game's title screen shows its version from the same notes file.
The home side is now the Wildcats, in navy, white and red to match the artwork.
Build order changed: online head-to-head moves up to right after play calling, and the league is built online-first so friends can coach rival schools from the first season.

notes.title: Kickoff: coach-only exhibition

items.text: A full four-quarter exhibition game. You call the plays; the AI controls all 22 players and coaches the other sideline.
Starter playbook: 8 offensive plays and 4 defensive calls, each with a diagram. Guess the offense right and your defense gets an edge.
Coach's decisions: punt, field goal, extra point or two-point try, and timeouts.
Watch at normal speed, fast, or skip to the result. Scoring plays and turnovers you fast-forwarded are replayed at normal speed.
Kickoffs, punts, field goals, safeties, interceptions, fumbles and sacks, with a score bug and a final summary.
Every game is reproducible from its seed and the list of coaching decisions, which is what will make online results fair.

notes.title: Design foundation

items.text: Game design, architecture plan, data model and acceptance criteria for every milestone.
Direction set: coach-only. Nobody steers a player; every decision is a coach's decision.

roadmap.title: Exhibition football
roadmap.text: Coach a full game against the AI. Playable now; waiting on playtest sign-off.

roadmap.title: Playbooks and smarter football
roadmap.text: A 24-play library, build-your-own book, four defensive fronts, fatigue and substitutions, a play clock and a game plan. Playable now.

roadmap.title: Online head-to-head
roadmap.text: Invite a friend with a game PIN and coach against each other live, with hidden play calls. Playable now on the website.

roadmap.title: Sideline voice chat
roadmap.text: Talk to the other coach during an online game, free and straight from your browser. Playable now on the website.

roadmap.title: Design your own plays
roadmap.text: Draw up offensive and defensive plays in an editor, test them on a practice field, and carry them into games. Playable now.

roadmap.title: Coach profile and Hall of Fame
roadmap.text: Career wins, losses and championships for every online coach, and a top-ten Hall of Fame. Records count now; championships arrive with dynasty seasons.

roadmap.title: The big playbook
roadmap.text: A 40-play starter book and 40 defensive calls. Playable now.

roadmap.title: Special teams
roadmap.text: Kickoff calls and going for the block. Playable now.

roadmap.title: Cut-ins
roadmap.text: Artwork for touchdowns, turnovers, kicks, half time and the final whistle. In the game now.

roadmap.title: Game length options
roadmap.text: Choose 4 to 12 minute quarters. Playable now.

roadmap.title: Weather
roadmap.text: Rain, wind, snow and heat. Playable now.

roadmap.title: Statistics and school records
roadmap.text: Box scores for every player, season and career numbers, league leaders, and a record book for every school with records that can be broken. Playable now in solo dynasty.

roadmap.title: Playoffs
roadmap.text: A bracket for the state title instead of first place hosting second.

roadmap.title: Coaching career
roadmap.text: Job offers from other schools after good seasons, the sack after bad ones, and a coaching record that follows you.

roadmap.title: Friends' leagues catch up
roadmap.text: Statistics, record books, awards and call-ups in a dynasty with friends.

roadmap.title: State leagues
roadmap.text: Pick any of the fifty states and get a league of eight invented schools with a seven-week schedule and standings. Playable now.

roadmap.title: Solo dynasty
roadmap.text: Season after season with one school: a state title game, rosters that turn over, a trophy case. Playable now.

roadmap.title: Dynasty with friends
roadmap.text: Friends coach rival schools in the same league. When two coaches meet, both have to be online to play; the week moves on when every game is in. Playable now.

roadmap.title: Overtime
roadmap.text: High school overtime from the ten-yard line. Playable now.

roadmap.title: Penalties and a realism scorecard
roadmap.text: Flags on the field, and the AI game held to real high school numbers by an automatic scorecard. In the game now.

roadmap.title: Returns
roadmap.text: Interception, fumble, kickoff and punt returns played out on the field with blocks and tackles. In the game now.

roadmap.title: Ball-carrier moves
roadmap.text: Stiff arms, trucks, jukes, spins and dives for backs, receivers and returners, driven by their ratings. Playable now.

roadmap.title: Audibles
roadmap.text: Change the play at the line after you see the defensive front, solo and online. Playable now.

roadmap.title: Freshmen, JV and varsity
roadmap.text: Players who age from freshman to senior, a JV squad that plays its own schedule, and call-ups to the varsity. Playable now in solo dynasty.

roadmap.title: Friday night atmosphere
roadmap.text: Chants, a pep band with a fight song for every school, a PA announcer, and half-time shows with homecoming and senior night. Playable now.

roadmap.title: A cleaner look
roadmap.text: One look across the menu, the game screen, the call sheet and the dynasty pages, taken from the supplied art. Playable now.

roadmap.title: Kids grow up
roadmap.text: Graduation, incoming freshmen from feeder schools, player development, morale and academics.

roadmap.title: Run the program
roadmap.text: Coaching staff, facilities, fundraising and community expectations.

roadmap.title: Playoffs and championships
roadmap.text: League, section and state brackets, with overtime.

roadmap.title: Commissioner tools
roadmap.text: Renaming schools and picking colors is in. Still to come: joining late, handing over a school and removing a coach.

roadmap.title: Records, alumni and legacy
roadmap.text: Record books, hall of fame, college offers, and a coaching career with job offers.

roadmap.title: Regional and national
roadmap.text: More states, showcase games, rankings and a fictional national championship.

roadmap.title: Friday night broadcast
roadmap.text: High-school broadcast look: score bug, lower-third graphics, player and stat overlays, replays worth watching. The AI-run football has to be sharp and fun to watch.
